docs.text: What is Polygon Crusher 9000? Polygon Crusher 9000 is a Blender add-on that makes heavy models light. It does two jobs: Decimate reduces the triangle count and keeps the shape, the shading, the textures and the hard edges. Remesh rebuilds the model as clean, even quads, at the quad count you ask for. You tell it what kind of model you have (a scan, an AI model, a CAD part, a character, a garment), how much you want left, and what to keep. The rest is automatic. The work runs in a separate process, so Blender stays responsive, and you can cancel at any time. Built for: 3D scans, sculpts, AI-generated models, hard-surface and CAD parts, clothing, and LODs for games. Get Started · What's New · Settings Reference · Limits Features Source type — pick Auto , Scan , AI , CAD , Hard Surface , Organic or Cloth , and the method for that kind of model is used. See Source Types . Decimate or Remesh — reduce triangles, or rebuild the model as quads. See Target Modes and Remesh . Keep what matters — Shading , Textures and, for hard-surface and CAD parts, Sharps . With Shading and Textures both off you get the shape only, closed and ready to 3D print. See Hard Surface and Sharps . Exact targets — ask for 80% and you get 80%. Ask for 5,000 triangles and you get 5,000. Remesh lands close to the quad count you ask for. Some options can stop a crush above the target, so check the report. See Limits . Three ways to set the amount — Percent , Count (per object), or Budget (one total for the whole selection). Quad Density — paint where you want smaller or larger quads. See Quad Density . Symmetry — a mirrored model stays mirrored, on X, Y or Z or the axis of its Mirror modifier. Show Hard Edges — see in the viewport which edges will be kept before you crush. See Show Hard Edges . Protect Areas — paint or select the parts that must keep their detail. See Protect Areas . Clean Mesh and Scan Repair — close cracks and holes, cut the floor, remove spikes. See Clean Mesh and Scan Repair . Import and Crush — crush an OBJ, PLY or STL file straight from disk, for scans too big for Blender's importers. See Import and Crush . Bake maps — bake a normal map and a base color map onto the result, with an Undo Bake button. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . LODs in one click — build a whole LOD chain from the original. See LODs . Rigs, shape keys and vertex colors carry over. See Rigs, Shape Keys and Vertex Colors . Revert — delete the result and bring back the original. See Keep Original and Revert . Modifier-aware — works on the evaluated mesh, so booleans, subdivision and the rest of the stack are included. The original keeps its modifiers. Live progress and Cancel — the main button becomes a progress bar and a Cancel button while it works. Requirements Blender 4.2 or later. 4.2 is the lowest version the extension accepts and has not been tested; the add-on is tested on the newest Blender OS Windows (x64), Linux (x64; ARM64 for Decimate), macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) Support Questions or issues? docs.text: Benchmarks: against Blender Decimate and meshoptimizer Note These numbers were measured on version 2.3.x (the meshoptimizer comparison on 2.7.1). They have not been re-measured for 2.12. Where it stands Two comparisons have been measured in full, both with the repo's own test harnesses, plus a first look at MeshLab on two small meshes. Nothing else has been, so this page makes no claims about Simplygon, InstaLOD, ZBrush Decimation Master or any other reducer. Against Blender Decimate (2026-10-10, engine 2.3.2): 2.2–3.0× faster on meshes of 1–7.5 million triangles, about even at 100k, slower (0.6×) on a scene of 103 small parts. The same shape at the same triangle count. Decimate also reaches its target, so exact counts are not what sets the two apart. Ahead on CAD with Hard Surface on (creases stay where they are), and on everything Decimate does not do: Keep Normals, UV-aware collapses, scan repair, Import and Crush, bakes, LOD chains, rigs and shape keys carried over. Behind with Keep UVs on a part cut into many small UV islands at a very low target, because seam vertices stay on their islands. Against meshoptimizer (2026-10-13, engine 2.7.1): The same surface error, within measurement noise, on scans, sculpts and smooth CAD at keep 10% and keep 2%; slightly lower on a small CAD block. On a hard-surface model of many parts the picture is mixed. Both tools' default settings stop short of the target on it; 2.7.1 fixed that for Polygon Crusher, and meshoptimizer's attribute setting still has the lower error at keep 10%. At keep 2% they are close. meshoptimizer is about three times faster, on one core; Polygon Crusher uses all cores. On a single core the gap would be wider. Against MeshLab (early readings, two meshes, see below): about the same at keep 10%; MeshLab's plain decimation is better on the small CAD block at keep 2%, and its UV-keeping variant is much worse there. In short: a match for the best open-source simplifier on surface error, slower per core, better integrated for Blender work, and since 2.7.1 no longer the tool that falls over on multi-part hard-surface models, without being the best one on those either. The sections below show the numbers. Against Blender Decimate Measured on 2026-10-10 with Polygon Crusher 2.3.2. This section shows how the speed figure on the store page was measured, so you can judge it yourself. These numbers still apply to 2.4.x. 2.4 changed the panel, the bake, and a Keep Normals correction that only runs on CAD and hard-surface parts. 2.4.2 added two small engine checks (no stray spike vertices, better detail in protected areas) that leave scan, sculpt and CAD results unchanged. 2.5.0 changed only the bake (base color from image textures, fewer tiny UV islands on scans); the crush itself is the same. 2.6.0 added Low Distortion under Keep UVs, which costs a few percent of crush time. 2.7.1 changed how kept edges and small pieces are handled; scans, sculpts and smooth CAD parts measure the same as before, hard-surface models with many parts do not (see Against meshoptimizer below). None of these were re-timed against Decimate. Summary Speed: 2.2–3.0× faster than Blender's Decimate on meshes of 1–7.5 million triangles. About the same at 100k. Slower on many small parts. Shape: about the same as Decimate at the same triangle count. On CAD parts with Hard Surface on, creases stay exactly in place. With Keep UVs on, very low targets on parts cut into many small UV islands keep less shape, because seam vertices stay on their islands. Imported scans: meshes imported from glTF or FBX are often split into separate pieces along their UV seams. Turn on Clean Mesh for these, or open edges can shrink and leave gaps. Method Blender 5.2.2 LTS, run headless. Windows 11, Intel i7-12700H (20 threads), 64 GB RAM. Blender: Decimate modifier in Collapse mode, ratio = target ÷ input, applied to a new mesh. Polygon Crusher: the add-on's own pipeline (read the mesh with UVs and normals, run the native engine with an exact target, build the result with UVs and custom normals). No bake. Time: end to end, median of 3 runs. Shape loss: distance from the original surface to the result, as % of the bounding-box diagonal (mean / max). Against meshoptimizer Measured on 2026-10-13, engine 2.7.0 and then 2.7.1, against meshoptimizer v1.3 (the open-source simplifier behind Godot and the glTF tools), built from source. One Windows machine. This is the test that found the two 2.7.1 fixes, so it is shown here with both results. Method The engine binary alone, not the add-on, on OBJ files: the 1.26M rock scan and the 98k boulder scan from above, a 60k noisy scan, the 1.0M sculpt, a 5k sculpt, the 5.1k CAD block, an 83k smooth CAD part, and an electricity pole of 103 parts (13.4k triangles). Targets: keep 10% and keep 2% of the triangles. Scans, sculpts and smooth CAD: the same error At keep 10%, mean error of the two tools, Polygon Crusher / meshoptimizer: Case Mean error (PC / mo) Worst (PC / mo) Rock scan 1.26M → 126k 0.069 / 0.069 0.16 / 0.16 Boulder scan 98k → 9.8k 0.123 / 0.127 0.28 / 0.28 Noisy scan 60k → 6k 0.173 / 0.182 0.58 / 0.48 Sculpt 1.0M → 101k 0.101 / 0.101 0.24 / 0.24 Smooth CAD part 83k → 8.3k 0.163 / 0.163 0.40 / 0.39 CAD block 5.1k → 512 0.163 / 0.188 0.38 / 0.52 Keep 2% looks the same: the two tools are within measurement noise of each other on every one of these, before and after 2.7.1. (The 1.26M scan and the 1.0M sculpt were only run with the 2.7.0 engine; 2.7.1 did not change the scan or sculpt path.) The multi-part pole: what 2.7.1 fixed The pole has borders, material edges, seams and sharp edges everywhere, and 103 separate pieces. It is where the old engine failed. Pole 13.4k, keep 2% Triangles Mean error Worst error PC 2.7.0, plain crush 268 2.48 20.7 PC 2.7.0, Hard Surface mode 7,081 (stalled at 53%) 0.21 3.3 PC 2.7.1, plain crush 266 0.75 5.2 PC 2.7.1, Hard Surface mode 266 0.42 4.2 meshoptimizer, defaults 2,788 (stopped at 21%) 0.27 5.9 meshoptimizer, attributes 260 0.39 5.7 At keep 2% the 2.7.0 plain crush disintegrated: whole beams went while small insulators stayed, hence a worst-case error of 20.7% of the model's size. In 2.7.1 every piece keeps a minimum until the budget is spent, and the worst case is 5.2%. Hard Surface mode on 2.7.0 stalled at about half the triangles at both targets (7,091 at keep 10%, 7,081 at keep 2%), because the kept edges were a hard lock. In 2.7.1 it reaches 1,337 and 266. meshoptimizer with its defaults also stops short on this model, at 2,816 triangles whatever you ask; with its attribute settings it reaches the count. At keep 10% that setting has the lowest error of all the runs (mean 0.17, worst 0.84, against 0.23 and 1.30 for Hard Surface mode). At keep 2% the two are close: lower mean for meshoptimizer, lower worst case for Polygon Crusher. On the 5.1k CAD block, Hard Surface mode at keep 10% halved its error (mean 0.31 → 0.16, worst 1.23 → 0.38) because the hole rims are no longer locked. At keep 2% it now reaches 102 triangles where 2.7.0 stopped at 272, and that costs shape: mean error 1.98 against 1.13 at the old, higher count. Reaching a very low count on a small part is a trade you choose by picking the target. Speed meshoptimizer is about three times faster: 0.8 s against 2.3 s on the 1.26M scan at keep 10%, 0.5 s against 1.3 s on the 1.0M sculpt. It gets there on one core; Polygon Crusher spreads its work over all of them. Both are well under the time Blender needs to build the result mesh. Limits of this test Engine against library, both run from Python on one Windows machine. The add-on's own read, build and bake steps are not included, and neither is any glTF or game-engine pipeline around meshoptimizer. meshoptimizer has more settings than the two tried here; a tuned run may do better on the pole. Error is a surface-distance measurement. It does not see shading, UV stretch or whether a hole is still round; look at the result. Against MeshLab: early readings MeshLab's Quadric Edge Collapse Decimation (through pymeshlab 2025.7) is the reducer most people run on scans outside game studios. It was added to the bake-off harness on 2026-10-13 and has so far been run on two of the eight fixtures, on Linux, with the 2.7.1 engine. Two small meshes are not a verdict; the full set, on the Windows machine used above, is still to come. Same error measure as the meshoptimizer section; Polygon Crusher with its mode's flags, MeshLab with the filter's defaults ("plain") and with the with-texture variant that keeps the UV layout ("UVs"). Case Polygon Crusher (mean / worst) MeshLab plain MeshLab UVs CAD block 5.1k → 512 0.163 / 0.38 0.169 / 0.41 0.50 / 4.0 CAD block 5.1k → 102 1.98 / 12.1 0.99 / 5.4 3.5 / 21.8 Sculpt 5.1k → 514 0.114 / 0.23 0.120 / 0.27 0.130 / 0.27 Sculpt 5.1k → 102 0.364 / 0.85 0.437 / 1.87 0.59 / 2.3 At keep 10% the two are within a few percent of each other on both meshes. At keep 2% on the CAD block MeshLab's plain decimation is clearly better: half the mean error, half the worst case. Polygon Crusher's Hard Surface mode is paying there for reaching 102 triangles while still favouring the kept edges; the plain crush (no edges kept) scores 1.63 / 10.2, also behind MeshLab. This is the one case so far where another tool is ahead on a plain surface-error measure, and it will be checked on the full set. Part of the gap is the 2.7.1 decision to always reach the count: the 2.7.0 engine stopped at 272 triangles on this block with a lower error than 2.7.1 gets at 102. Keep 2% of a 5,000-triangle part is 102 triangles, which is below where either tool keeps the shape; on a part this small, pick the target by looking at the result, not the percentage. MeshLab's UV-keeping variant is far worse on the CAD block at both targets: the seams constrain it the way Keep UVs constrains any simplifier, and this block has many of them. On the sculpt Polygon Crusher is ahead at both targets, more so at keep 2%. Times are not comparable yet: a different machine from the rest of this page, and meshes this small finish in a few hundredths of a second either way.

docs.text: Limits Polygon Crusher 9000 does not always reach the target. This page lists what can stop it, and what the report tells you. After every crush, Blender's status bar shows a report: triangles before and after, time taken, and any warnings. Always check the "after" count. The result can stop above the target The crush aims for your target, but some things stop it early: Protect Area. Strong protection on large areas can leave the result above the target. Broken geometry. Duplicate or zero-area faces block collapses. Clean Mesh runs by itself on meshes with many duplicate vertices or zero-area triangles. Otherwise the report says the mesh may be broken and suggests Clean Mesh . If Clean Mesh is already on, it says the mesh cannot be reduced further without breaking its shape. The report only raises this warning when the result is clearly above the target (more than 20% over), so small differences do not show up as warnings. Kept edges (hard edges, material borders, UV seams) do not stop a crush above the target: a kept edge is a cost, not a lock. What a very low target costs on such a model is shape, not triangles: see What a very low target costs . Small pieces at heavy reductions A model made of many separate pieces (a pole with its insulators, a set of screws) loses whole pieces when the target is a small fraction of its triangles. Since 2.7.1 every connected piece keeps a minimum number of triangles until the error budget is truly spent, and then pieces go in order of how little they matter, smallest first. At an extreme target pieces still disappear; raise the target, or put a Protect Area on the ones that must stay. Small Pieces under Clean Mesh is a different thing: it deletes loose bits before the crush, on purpose. Objects can be skipped An object is left untouched, and named in the report, when it: has no geometry after modifiers, has fewer than 4 triangles, or gets no triangles in a Budget crush. If every selected object is already at or below the target, the copies are left unchanged and the report says so. Scans and noisy meshes: hard edges On a scan-like mesh, almost every edge has a small bend because of surface noise. Treating all of them as sharp would lock the whole mesh. So the Scan , Organic and Cloth sources do not keep angle-sharp edges, and on a model that reads as a scan under another source, angle-based detection is skipped as well. Only the edges you marked Sharp in Blender are kept. Show Hard Edges says "Looks like a scan: only marked Sharp kept". If you want specific edges kept on a scan, mark them Sharp yourself first. Sharps Sharps is skipped on sources over 1 million triangles. On a low-poly model where bevel edges cover most of the surface (a game weapon), the bevels ease off so the shape is still followed. For crisp hard edges there, use Decimate rather than Remesh. A hard-surface source falls back to the usual method (not the HiPoly-style one) with Textures on, several materials, Symmetry, protected areas, keeping under 5%, or low-poly kits it cannot bring down to the target. See Source Types . Very low targets on dense CAD Very low targets on dense CAD meshes, a few hundred triangles, can fold the walls of holes together. This leaves edges that are shared by three or more faces (non-manifold edges). The report warns when a crushed copy has more of these edges than its source. If that matters for your export or for baking, raise the target. Remesh Remesh makes quads (and, on models of many loose parts, some triangles joined into quads). It lands close to the count you ask for, usually within a few percent. A CAD part with many holes can need more quads than you asked for (a block with many holes needs at least about 1,240); the status line says so. A quad remesh rounds off fine detail finer than a quad. On low-poly hard surface with many bevels, Decimate keeps hard edges crisper. Thin walls and bars at low counts can tear. Models that are not one clean surface (triangle soups, self-crossing sheets) can fail or come out as loose pieces. Switch on Rebuild Surface for those: it rebuilds a closed skin, but loses detail finer than its grid and your Sharp marks. Remesh does not use LODs, Clean Mesh, Protect, Import and Crush or the flat-area options. The quad engine's result differs slightly between processor types (Apple Silicon vs Intel). The same computer always gives the same mesh. On Linux ARM64 there is no quad engine, so only Decimate is available. Quad Density: a part smaller than a big quad loses its shape under Less Detail . Baking Base Color is baked from the image textures feeding each material's Base Color, or from vertex colors when a material has none. Colors made by procedural nodes (Noise, Gradient, a plain color value) are not baked. An object with neither textures nor vertex colors is skipped for Base Color, and the report says so. A bake needs UVs on the crushed mesh. Meshes without UVs are unwrapped automatically. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . The baked maps are connected in copies of the materials. If an input was already connected there, the old link is replaced. The bake happens after the crush. A failed bake is listed in the report as a note and the crushed mesh is kept. Rigs, shape keys and vertex colors Skin weights, the Armature modifier, shape keys and vertex colors carry over to the crushed copy, with a few limits: shape keys are dropped when a modifier changes the vertex count, and vertex colors are skipped on sources over 3 million triangles. See Rigs, Shape Keys and Vertex Colors . Textures (Keep UVs) Textures is off by default. Turn it on only when the result must keep its UV layout. UV transfer quality depends on how much the topology changed. Moderate reductions give the cleanest results. UV seams are held in place and collapses that would fold a face's texture mapping are refused. The crush relaxes those rules in stages once it runs out of safe collapses, so the target is reached; the last few percent of a very low target can then show some stretch near seams. Revert Revert needs the original. It only works when the crush was made with Keep Original on, or with LODs. See Keep Original and Revert . Import and Crush Reads .obj , .ply (ascii and binary) and .stl (ascii and binary). Other formats (glTF, FBX, USD) have to go through Blender's own importer. Normals in the file are ignored; the result is shaded smooth. Shading, Protect, Bake and LODs do not apply to an imported file. A texture is only connected when the image is next to the model and Keep UVs (and textures) is on. Textures other than the base color ( map_Kd ) are not read. Faces with more than four corners are split as fans. A concave n-gon can come out wrong; scans do not have those. Memory: the engine needs about 1 GB of RAM per 3 million triangles in the file. A 32 million triangle OBJ (2.5 GB on disk) peaked at 10 GB and crushed to 200,000 triangles in 72 seconds. On a 16 GB machine, stay under about 40 million triangles. Platform Blender 4.2 or later. 4.2 is the lowest version the extension accepts and has not been tested; the add-on is tested on Blender 5.2. Windows x64, Linux x64, Linux ARM64, macOS Apple Silicon and macOS Intel have a bundled Decimate engine. Remesh (the quad engine) is bundled for Windows x64, Linux x64 and macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), not for Linux ARM64. The add-on needs its native binary. There is no Python fallback. If the binary is missing, the panel shows "Native binary not found" and Crush does not run.

docs.text: Settings Reference All settings are in the Polygon Crusher 9000 tab of the 3D Viewport sidebar (press N ). The panel goes top to bottom in four steps, then a collapsed Advanced section holds the rest. Settings that do not apply to the chosen source or tool are hidden, not greyed out, so the panel only shows what the next run will use. Status line At the very bottom of the tab, the Selection line says what is selected: the number of meshes and their triangle total. With nothing selected it says "Select a mesh object to start". 1 Source Seven buttons — default Auto What kind of model this is: Auto , Scan , AI , CAD , Hard Surface , Organic , Cloth . Picking one uses the method for that kind and sets a starting amount. With Auto, a line under the buttons says Last run treated it as: ... after a run. See Source Types . 2 Output Decimate / Remesh Two tabs — default Decimate Decimate reduces the triangles and keeps the shape, shading and textures. Remesh rebuilds the model as clean, even quads. See Remesh (Quads) . Percent, Count, Budget Three buttons — default Percent Percent — remove a share of the triangles. Count — each selected object is crushed to a count. Budget — one total for the whole selection. See Target Modes . The control below the buttons changes with the choice: Reduction (Percent): 1% to 99%, default 50% (the source sets a starting value). Dragging covers 5% to 95%. Target Triangles (Count): minimum 4, default 5000 . An object with fewer triangles than this is left at its own count. Total Triangles (Budget): minimum 4, default 100,000 . The result never has fewer than 4 triangles. Under the control, a readout shows before → after triangles (or tris → quads for Remesh), added up over the selected meshes. The "after" number is the target, not a promise. See Limits . 3 Keep Shading Toggle — default on The result takes the original's smooth shading, so it does not look faceted, even when the topology changes a lot. Leave it on for almost all cases. Textures Toggle — default off Keeps the UV layout and materials so textures still fit the result. UV seams are held in place, and the crush refuses collapses that would fold the texture mapping. It does nothing if the mesh has no UVs. Sharps Toggle — default on ; shows for Hard Surface and CAD only Hard edges stay in place and crisp, including small-bevel corners. See Hard Surface and Sharps . Shape only With Shading and Textures both off, you get the shape only: a closed mesh ready to 3D print. The panel says so. Rebuild Surface (Remesh only) Checkbox — default off For hopeless input (triangle soups, open or self-crossing models). Rebuilds a closed skin first, then remeshes it. See Remesh (Quads) . Remesh status After a Remesh, a box under the Keep row says what the run did: the real quad count, the share of quads and any notes. 4 Crush Symmetry Toggle + X / Y / Z — default off , axis X Keeps a mirrored model mirrored: both halves are treated the same way and the center line stays straight and closed. The axis is the object's own X, Y or Z through its origin, like Blender's Mirror modifier. If the object has an active Mirror modifier, its axis is used instead and the axis buttons are greyed out. With Remesh , one half is remeshed and mirrored. Not used by Budget or Import and Crush . Crush The main button. It does the job of the tab you chose ( Crush LODs while LODs is on). It is available when at least one mesh is selected. While it works, the button becomes Cancel with a progress bar. Click Cancel or press ESC to stop. Revert The small icon next to Crush. Deletes the selected result and brings back its original. Greyed out when there is nothing to revert. See Keep Original and Revert . Import and Crush... Button (Decimate only) Opens a file browser for an .obj , .ply or .stl file. See Import and Crush . Also in File → Import . Keep Original warning When Keep Original is off, a red line under the button says so: "Original will be deleted" (Decimate) or "Keep Original is off: Revert won't work" (Remesh). When the native binary is missing, the panel shows "Native binary not found" and Crush refuses to run. See Troubleshooting . Advanced Click Advanced to open it. It starts collapsed in every session. It has four boxes. Result Keep Original (default on ) — the original is hidden instead of deleted. Greyed out while LODs is on. See Keep Original and Revert . Combine Elements (default off ) — joins all the selected meshes into one, welds the parts that touch or overlap, and crushes the result once into a single object. Edges Hard Edge Angle (default 30° ) with the eye button — the eye is Show Hard Edges . Hidden for Organic, Scan and Cloth sources. See Show Hard Edges . Tidy Flat Areas (Decimate only; Auto, CAD, Hard Surface) — flips long thin triangles on flat areas into even ones. No point moves. Flat Areas as Quads (Decimate only; Auto, CAD, Hard Surface) — merges the triangles of each flat area into one face and pairs the rest into quads. Leave it off for game exports that need triangles. Extra Steps Each one opens its options right under it while ticked. LODs (Decimate only) — Levels (1 to 8, default 3) and Ratio (5% to 95%, default 50%). See LODs . Clean Mesh (Decimate only) — Small Pieces (0% to 5%, default 0.1%), and the Scan Repair switches: Cut Floor (with Height or the Pick Floor eyedropper), Remove Spikes , Fill Holes (with Size , 0.1% to 50%, default 5%). The repair switches show for Auto, Scan and AI. See Clean Mesh and Scan Repair . Bake to Textures — Normal Map , Base Color , Undo Bake , Bake Into Kept UVs (Remesh with Textures on), Size (512, 1K, 2K, 4K, default 2K), Normal Y (OpenGL or DirectX), Save To (Blend File Folder or Custom Folder). See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Quad Density (Remesh only) — More Detail , Less Detail , Done Painting , Strength (1 to 8, default 3). See Quad Density . Protect (Decimate only) — Paint Protect , Done Painting , Add and Remove (Edit Mode), a vertex group field, Strength (0% to 100%, default 50%), Blur (0% to 100%, default 5%) and Show Heatmap . See Protect Areas . Last Crush Shown after a Decimate, for the active crushed object: Object — the crushed object's name. Triangles — before → after. Total time and Passes . Click Details for the time of each phase (Extract, Write, Crush, Read, Build, Bake Normals). "Bake Normals" here is the shading transfer, not the normal map bake. When several objects are selected they run at the same time, so the phase times can add up to more than the clock time. The numbers are only kept for the current Blender session. Remembered settings The amount, Hard Edge Angle, LOD and bake size settings are remembered across files and Blender restarts for new scenes. A file that already has Polygon Crusher settings keeps its own.

docs.text: Toggle + X / Y / Z — default off , axis X Keeps a mirrored model mirrored: both halves are treated the same way and the center line stays straight and closed. docs.text: The main button. It does the job of the tab you chose ( Crush LODs while LODs is on). It is available when at least one mesh is selected. While it works, the button becomes Cancel with a progress bar. Click Cancel or press ESC to stop.

docs.text: Click Advanced to open it. It starts collapsed in every session. It has four boxes.

docs.text: Keep Original (default on ) — the original is hidden instead of deleted. Greyed out while LODs is on. See Keep Original and Revert . docs.text: Hard Edge Angle (default 30° ) with the eye button — the eye is Show Hard Edges . Hidden for Organic, Scan and Cloth sources. See Show Hard Edges . docs.text: Each one opens its options right under it while ticked. LODs (Decimate only) — Levels (1 to 8, default 3) and Ratio (5% to 95%, default 50%). See LODs . docs.text: Shown after a Decimate, for the active crushed object: Object — the crushed object's name. Triangles — before → after. Total time and Passes . docs.text: Troubleshooting "Native binary not found" The addon ships with platform-specific simplifier binaries in its bin/ folder ( simplify-win-x86_64.exe , simplify-darwin-arm64 , simplify-darwin-x86_64 , simplify-linux-x86_64 , simplify-linux-arm64 ). The operator refuses to run if it can't find a binary matching your platform. If you see this: Re-install the addon from the official .zip — do not copy files manually Check that the binary exists at: <Blender extensions folder>/polygon_crusher_9000/bin/simplify-<your-platform> On macOS / Linux, the executable bit is restored automatically at runtime, but if your installer stripped it entirely, re-installing usually fixes it. There is no Python fallback. The result has more triangles than my target This is the most common question. Read the report in Blender's status bar. It shows the actual triangle count and usually says why. See Limits for the full list. The usual causes: "the mesh may be broken: try Clean Mesh" — duplicate or zero-area faces blocked the crush. Turn on Clean Mesh and crush again. "it can't be reduced further without breaking the shape" — Clean Mesh was already on. The mesh is at its limit for this shape. Protect with a high Strength on a large area can leave the result above the target. Lower the Strength. A hole came out as a pentagon, or a crease flattened The target was too low for the number of edges you asked to keep. The crush reaches the count you asked for even on CAD and Hard Surface, so at a very low count some kept lines have to give way. It picks the ones that change the shape least. Raise the target, raise Hard Edge Angle (Advanced → Edges), or put a Protect Area on the part that must stay. See Hard Surface Preservation . Small parts disappeared At a heavy reduction the budget runs out and whole pieces go. Since 2.7.1 every separate piece keeps a minimum number of triangles until nothing else is left to remove, and then the smallest pieces go first; before, pieces went in whatever order they happened to collapse. Raise the target, or protect the pieces that must stay. If pieces are missing right after Clean Mesh , lower Small Pieces : it deletes loose bits on purpose. See Limits . Hard edges kept almost nothing on my scan On a scan-like mesh, and with the Scan, Organic or Cloth source, angle-based detection is skipped, because surface noise would make almost every edge sharp. Only edges you marked Sharp are kept. Mark the edges you want to keep as Sharp in Blender, then crush again. Show Hard Edges shows what is kept. See Limits . The report warns about non-manifold edges Very low targets on dense CAD meshes can fold hole walls together, leaving edges shared by three or more faces. Raise the target. See Limits . Crushed mesh looks faceted Shading (under Keep) was probably off. Turn it on and crush again. If you baked a Normal Map , the crushed mesh uses its own smooth shading and the normal map carries the detail. Make sure the normal map is connected in the crushed mesh's material and the viewport is in Material Preview or Rendered mode. My baked maps do not show Workbench cannot show textures or normal maps. Crush switches a Workbench scene to EEVEE for you and tells you in the report. If you changed it back, switch the viewport to Material Preview. Base Color comes from the image textures feeding Base Color in the original's materials, or from vertex colors. If the report says an object has "no image texture or vertex colors", no base color was baked for it. A texture reported as "not loaded" is missing on disk: fix its path on the original and crush again. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Use Undo Bake (Advanced → Bake to Textures) to remove a bake and try again. Look in the folder you chose under Save To . For an unsaved .blend, the maps are packed into the file instead of saved as PNG files. Crusher ignored my modifiers It shouldn't — Polygon Crusher always reads the evaluated (post-modifier) mesh. If the result still looks like the un-modified base mesh, check that the modifier is actually visible in the viewport (the camera/eye toggles in the modifier properties panel). Anything hidden in the viewport is hidden from Polygon Crusher too. Blender freezes during crush Polygon Crusher runs the heavy work in a separate process, so Blender should stay responsive. If the UI freezes: Very large meshes can take real time. Give it a few seconds. The progress bar under the Crush button updates as the run goes: if it is still moving, the run is healthy. Click Cancel (the Crush button while it runs) or press ESC to stop. Where did my crushed object go? All crushed outputs are linked into a Crushed collection at the scene root (created automatically on the first crush). LOD chains go into a <name>_LODs collection inside it. The original object is either hidden (default) or deleted, depending on Keep Original . The Revert button is greyed out Revert needs a selected crushed object whose original still exists. It is greyed out when: the crushed object is not selected (the hidden original is not enough), the crush was made with Keep Original off, or you deleted the original. It is also greyed out while a crush is running. See Keep Original and Revert . Last Crush says there are no stats Last Crush (in Advanced) only shows Decimate results for the active crushed object, from the current Blender session. If you select the original (or anything else), it says "No stats for" that object. Click a crushed object in the Crushed collection to see its timings. Remesh says the quad engine is not available The quad engine is bundled for Windows x64, Linux x64 and macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel). On Linux ARM64 only Decimate works. On the other systems, re-install the add-on from the official .zip : the panel names the missing file. Remesh: the result is not what I expected The status box under Keep says the real count and what happened. If it had to spend more quads to avoid damage, it says that too. A CAD part with many holes needs a minimum number of quads for a clean grid. The status says how many. Models that are not one clean surface (triangle soups, self-crossing sheets) may need Rebuild Surface (under Keep, Remesh only). Hard edges on a low-poly model with many bevels come out crisper with Decimate. See Remesh (Quads) . Contact Support Still having trouble? Email henriquevlopes@gmail.com

docs.text: What's New Everything that changed since 2.8.0, grouped by theme, newest first. The current version is 2.12.20 . A new panel in four steps (2.9.3 to 2.11.24) The panel was rebuilt to ask only what matters. Source (2.11.24) replaces the old Mode menu. Say what the model is (Auto, Scan, AI, CAD, Hard Surface, Organic or Cloth) and the right method is used, each starting at a sensible amount. See Source Types . Decimate and Remesh tabs (2.11.1) replace the old Quads checkbox. The button below follows the tab. Keep: Shading, Textures (and Sharps for hard-surface sources). With both Shading and Textures off, you get the shape only, closed and ready to 3D print. Everything else is under Advanced , in four calm boxes (2.9.9): Result, Edges, Extra Steps and Last Crush. Own sidebar tab (2.8.1). The panel has its own Polygon Crusher 9000 tab and remembers whether you left it open. The Mode menu is gone (2.9.3). UV seams follow Textures, and the Low Distortion and Percent preset boxes were removed. Nothing changes by itself any more. Red warnings (2.9.4, 2.11.7): problems show in red, and a red line tells you when Keep Original is off. Show Hard Edges works on every model (2.9.3), not only CAD. Subdivision Cage was removed (2.9.3). It did not work well enough. Remesh: clean quads at the count you ask for (2.9.0 to 2.12.19) Remesh (first called Quadify) rebuilds a model as even quads. It arrived in 2.9.0 and has been improved in nearly every release since. See Remesh (Quads) . The count is the count (2.9.0, 2.12.3). It searches for the setting that lands on your number and tells you the real count. On models where the engine leaves tears to patch, the average miss fell from 8.6% to 2.3%. Quad Density (2.12.0, 2.12.1). Paint where you want smaller quads ( More Detail ) or larger quads ( Less Detail ). The total stays the same. See Quad Density . Symmetry in Remesh. One half is remeshed and mirrored, so the seam runs straight down the middle. Rebuild Surface (2.12.4): for triangle soups and models whose surfaces run through each other. The Thingiverse triangle soup that came back as 2,805 loose pieces now comes back as one closed, all-quad piece. Sharp edges steer the quads (2.12.5). On a 5-million-triangle gun body the quads follow 98% of the sharp edges (it was 7%). CAD parts get a clean grid (2.11.4, 2.11.6, 2.12.8, 2.12.18, 2.12.19): flat faces stay flat, every hole is a closed round loop, quad loops run along the hard edges, and the quads on flat faces are evened out (badly skewed quads around holes fell from about 3 to 8% to about 1%). Auto no longer needs a switch, and Hard Surface tries the grid first. Very low counts get a coarser all-quad grid. Models of many parts keep every part (2.11.14, 2.11.15, 2.12.6, 2.12.9). Big parts are remeshed one by one, and small parts are simplified and paired into quads, so nothing vanishes. On the game weapon: all parts kept, 89% quads, near the asked count, no broken edges, and faster. The 1,862-part electric pole kit loses nothing. Sewn garments are sewn together and remeshed in one run (2.12.7). The denim jacket comes back in 8 pieces instead of 32. Broken 3D-print models (2.11.16 to 2.11.21): faces pointing both ways are turned to agree, zero-area flat plates are kept, thin walls and bars stay closed at low counts, and models of surfaces running through each other are rebuilt first. A chair that came back in shreds is now clean, in half the time. UVs, materials, vertex colors and baking. Remesh carries UVs and materials and bakes by itself when seams would crack (2.9.x to 2.11.x), and keeps vertex colors (2.10.1). Much faster. A 1-million-triangle sculpt went from 12 minutes to 8 seconds, a 9-million-triangle scan from 13 minutes to about 1.5 minutes, and CAD parts take 2 to 4 seconds (2.11.0). Scans are 30% faster again in 2.12.9. Progress and no freezes (2.11.8, 2.11.22). The button becomes a progress bar (Reading, Preparing, Remeshing, Building, Shading, Baking) and Blender keeps redrawing. A stuck engine is stopped. It repairs damage (2.9.2): if a remesh tears a closed model, it tries again with more quads. It also tells torn models apart from shattered thin parts, and gives the right advice for each. Works on Windows, Linux and Intel Macs (2.9.1, 2.9.2). The result after a Remesh is selected and active (2.11.7). Keeping hard edges: Sharps (2.12.16 to 2.12.20) Sharps (2.12.16): a toggle in Keep for Hard Surface and CAD. Hard edges, including corners modelled with a small bevel, stay in place and crisp after Decimate or Remesh. Rounded fillets stay smooth. See Hard Surface and Sharps . Remesh with Sharps (2.12.17): small round holes come out round, not pinched into stars, and nothing folds. Heavily bevelled models (2.12.20): when bevels cover most of a low-poly model (the game weapon), they ease off so the result still follows the shape. Hard Surface decimates with a better method (2.11.25): rounded bevels keep their rows, flat areas become big clean triangles, and a 5-million-triangle gun body takes half the time. Show Hard Edges (2.9.3): see the kept edges in the viewport before you crush. Cyan for marked Sharp, yellow for angle edges, purple for material borders, red for UV seams, green for open borders. See Show Hard Edges . Scans, cracks and holes (2.11.9 to 2.12.20) Fill Holes closes the cracks in scans (2.11.10 to 2.11.13). Thin cracks between scan patches are zipped shut, with no visible crack lines. A noisy rock scan comes out closed except for its outer ground edge. Surfaces are no longer glued together, and seams are not capped as if they were holes. Flat openings of any size are capped (2.9.3), such as the end of a pipe. Pick Floor (2.11.9): click a point on the model to set where Cut Floor cuts. A blue plane follows the mouse. See Clean Mesh and Scan Repair . Scans keep their shading and fine detail (2.12.20). Before, Fill Holes could scramble the shading, and fine detail could flatten. Scans also stop wasting triangles on texture-atlas seams. Scan and AI sources switch on the repairs by themselves (2.11.24) and are 10 to 40% faster than Auto. Rocks no longer tear in Remesh (2.11.15). Cloth (2.11.15 to 2.12.20) Folds are no longer stiff (2.12.20). On soft cloth (the goose puffer) the shape error is less than half of before. Thick cloth lands on the count you ask for (2.12.20): 50,000 asked gave 58,700, now 50,100, with no dark patches. Denim-style garments remesh cleanly, and dark shading flips on cloth are fixed (2.11.15). Textures and baking (2.9.x to 2.11.x) Undo Bake takes a bake back off an object: the old materials return and the baked images are deleted. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Bake Into Kept UVs for Remesh. No more black textures from missing image files (2.10.1): a material whose image can't be found is left as it is. Crush with textures no longer turns poles into spikes (2.11.15), when a model's UVs are cut into many tiny islands. Shading and quality of Decimate (2.8.2 to 2.12.20) Every test model is as good as or better than 2.8.0 (2.12.20): checked on 16 models, whole and close up, with textures. No more streaks or cracks on CAD (2.8.2). Thin triangles around holes no longer flip over or pick up the hole wall's shading. No stray Sharp edges (2.11.2, 2.11.3): the Sharp edges on the result are the real hard edges, and shading matches the original exactly. Crush no longer glues surfaces together (2.11.12). No more light teeth on low cylinders (2.10.0). Models with faces pointing both ways keep clean shading (2.11.19). Zero-area triangles no longer tear rims (2.11.16). Speed and big models (2.9.6 to 2.11.22) One fast Crush method (2.10.0): up to a third faster on big meshes (a 9-million-triangle scan: 42 s to 28 s). The old Fast Crush checkbox is gone because it is always on. Big meshes no longer freeze at 99% (2.11.x), and the slow preparation steps run in small pieces so the progress bar keeps moving (2.11.22). Cancel : the Crush button becomes Cancel while it runs. Esc still works. Selection stays tidy : after a Remesh the new mesh is selected. Platforms (2.8.3 to 2.9.2) Intel Macs work (2.8.3 for Decimate, 2.9.1 for Remesh). Linux gets the quad engine (2.9.2). The Windows quad engine ships in the current build. Retired Mode menu (Auto, Scan, Sculpt, Hard Surface, Custom): replaced by Source. Percent presets and saved presets. Low Distortion, UV Seams and Preserve checkboxes : now automatic. Fast Crush checkbox : always on. Subdivision Cage. Quadify options (Size by Edge Length, Follow Selected Edges, Mirror, Cloth Panels, Show Lines, Auto Creases, Best Quality, Detail Density, Smoothing, Retry, CAD Model): Remesh does these by itself now. Hard Surface Preservation checkboxes (Borders, Materials, Sharp Edges): now automatic, with Sharps and Hard Edge Angle for control.

docs.text: Bake Maps and Auto UVs Crush can bake the original's detail onto the low-poly copy as texture maps. It connects the maps in the copy's materials, so the result looks right straight away. Tick Bake to Textures in Advanced → Extra Steps . It shows two toggle buttons: Normal Map — bakes the original's surface detail. Base Color — bakes the original's color: its image textures, or its vertex colors. You can turn on one or both. Then click Crush as usual, in Decimate or in Remesh. After the crush, the progress bar shows "Baking" while the maps are made. Undo Bake When a selected object has a bake, an Undo Bake button appears under the map buttons. It takes the bake back off: the materials from before the bake return, and the baked images and the bake's own UV map are deleted. The mesh itself stays as it is. Bake Into Kept UVs (Remesh) With Remesh and Textures on, a Bake Into Kept UVs switch appears. It bakes into the UV layout the new quads already carry, instead of making a fresh unwrap. If the carried UVs come out too distorted, a fresh unwrap is made anyway. Remesh also bakes by itself when the UV seams would leave cracks (models from Meshy and similar tools often have a black or cracked baked atlas). Normal Map Bakes the original's surface detail into a normal map on the crushed mesh's UVs. The crushed mesh uses its own smooth shading instead of the Shading transfer from the original. This is what game engines expect. Normal Y picks the green channel convention. OpenGL (default) is for Blender, Unity and Godot. DirectX is for Unreal. A DirectX map still looks correct in Blender. The normal map is saved as Non-Color data. Base Color Bakes the original's color into a base color map on the crushed mesh's UVs, so a textured scan crushed to a fraction of its triangles still looks like the scan. Image textures first. For each material, the image feeding Base Color (directly, or through color nodes such as Mix or Hue/Saturation) is sampled through the original's own UVs. Materials with several textures are handled one by one, so a multi-material object gets one map with all of them in place. Vertex colors otherwise. A material with no image uses the object's active color attribute instead. Scans and ZBrush polypaint keep their color this way. Objects with neither are skipped, and the report says "no image texture or vertex colors". A texture whose file is missing is reported as "not loaded" and skipped. Auto UVs Baking needs UVs on the crushed mesh. Most scans and AI models have none, so Crush makes them. When: the original has no UVs, or Textures is off. How: the mesh is split into a few large, projection-based islands. Each island is flattened, given equal texel density, and packed with a margin that fits the map size. Ask first: when an original has no UVs, Crush shows a dialog first: "No UVs to bake onto" with a Auto UV and Crush button. The dialog lists the objects that have no UVs. If Textures is off, the crushed copy is unwrapped without a dialog. The report lists how many UV charts were made for each object. When baking, the borders of the UV islands are marked as seams and Sharp on the crushed mesh. This splits the smooth shading along the seams, so the normal map bakes without visible seams. If the original already has UVs and Textures is on, those UVs are used for the bake. Overlapping UVs A bake writes each pixel of the map once. If two faces share the same UV space (stacked or mirrored islands, common in game assets), they fight over those pixels and the map is wrong there. With Textures on, Crush checks for this and the report says so: it names the objects and how much of their map overlaps, and suggests turning Textures off so the crushed copy is baked onto new UVs. Where the maps go Save To has two choices: Blend File Folder (default) — maps are saved as PNG files in the same folder as the .blend file. If the file is unsaved, the maps are packed into the .blend instead. The panel shows "Unsaved: maps get packed". Custom Folder — maps are saved as PNG files in the folder you pick. A path that starts with // is relative to the .blend file. Files are named <object name>_normal.png and <object name>_basecolor.png . Size sets the map resolution: 512, 1K, 2K (default) or 4K. How the maps are connected Each crushed mesh gets its own copies of its materials, named <object name>_<material name> . Your original materials are not changed. If the mesh has no material, Crush makes one. The normal map goes through a Normal Map node into the Principled BSDF Normal input. The base color map goes into Base Color . If an input was already connected in the copy, the old link is replaced. The report says how many inputs were replaced. Viewport Workbench cannot show textures or normal maps. If the render engine is Workbench, Crush switches the scene to EEVEE and puts Solid-mode 3D views into Material Preview. The report says when it did this. See also Limits for what baking cannot do.
docs.title: Bake Maps and Auto UVs

docs.text: Rigs, Shape Keys and Vertex Colors The crushed copy keeps what the original carried per vertex. You don't need to re-rig, re-paint or re-bake anything. This happens on every Decimate, LOD and Budget part, with no setting to turn on. Remesh keeps vertex colors and, with Textures on, UVs and materials. What carries over Vertex groups (skin weights). Every group of the original, with its weights. Armature modifier and parent. The crushed copy gets the same Armature modifier (same rig, same options) and the same parent as the original, so it poses, animates and moves with the rig. Shape keys. Every key with its value, slider range, relative key and vertex group mask. Vertex colors. The active color attribute: scan colors, ZBrush polypaint, AI-model colors. Each new vertex takes its values from the nearest point on the original's surface, so weights, shapes and colors stay smooth across the crushed mesh. Crushing a posed character You can crush a character in any pose, or with shape keys dialed in. The add-on reads the original in its rest shape (the Armature modifier and the shape key mix are switched off for a moment and restored right away), so the crushed copy is made from the rest mesh and its own rig poses it. The pose is not baked in twice. On a test character crushed from 18,000 to 3,000 triangles mid-pose, the crushed copy stayed within 0.1% of the character's height of the original on average, in every pose tested. Limits Shape keys need the same vertex list. If a modifier changes the vertex count (Subdivision, Mirror, Remesh, Boolean...), shape keys can't be matched and are not carried. The current shape key mix is then crushed into the copy as it looks. Weights, the rig and colors still carry over. Vertex colors on huge meshes. Sources over 3 million triangles skip the vertex color step, and the report says so. Bake Base Color instead (see Bake Maps and Auto UVs ). Rigs and shape keys are still carried at any size. Envelope-only rigs. An Armature modifier that deforms by bone envelopes, with no vertex groups on the mesh, is not carried: the crushed copy keeps the pose it had at the time of the crush. Very low targets merge nearby details, so weights at tight spots (fingers, eyelids) follow the coarser mesh. Check the deformation at extreme poses.

docs.text: Clean Mesh and Scan Repair AI-generated and scanned meshes often have broken geometry. When you crush them, they fall apart into fragments or stop far above the target. Clean Mesh repairs the mesh before the crush. Turn it on with the Clean Mesh checkbox in Advanced → Extra Steps (Decimate only). The Scan and AI sources turn it on for you. It is also switched on by the Shape only setting (Shading and Textures both off), so a 3D print comes out closed. When the source stops asking for it, it goes back to what you had. What it does Merges duplicate vertices. Removes broken faces (zero-area faces) and duplicate faces. Fixes flipped faces. Deletes small floating pieces (floaters). Remove Small Pieces The Remove Small Pieces slider (labelled Small Pieces in the panel) sets how small a loose piece has to be to get deleted. It is a share of the mesh's triangles. Default: 0.1% . Range: 0% to 5%. 0% keeps every piece. Greyed out unless Clean Mesh is on. Raise it when a scan has lots of floating bits. Keep it low for models that really are made of separate parts, like a set of small screws. Runs on its own when a mesh needs it You don't always have to switch it on. Clean Mesh runs by itself on an object (and the report says so) when: 2% or more of its vertices are duplicates. Scans from glTF, FBX and OBJ are often split along UV seams; crushing them without welding opens cracks along the seams. 2% or more of its triangles have no area. This is typical of an OBJ saved with too few decimals, or a scan snapped to a coarse grid. Without cleaning, the crush would stop with "Unable to reduce mesh". Welded meshes (most CAD parts and sculpts) score 0% and are left alone. Turn the checkbox on yourself for other broken meshes, for example flipped faces or floating debris. Scan Repair Scans bring their own kind of damage that welding does not touch. Under Clean Mesh there are three switches for it. They show for the Auto , Scan and AI sources, work with a Decimate from the panel and with Import and Crush , and the report says what they did. Cut Floor The table, turntable or ground captured under the model is removed. With Height at 0% the floor is found by itself: it is the dense, flat layer at the very bottom of the model. If the scan has no such layer, nothing is cut and the report says no floor found . Set Height to cut at a share of the model's height instead (everything below that goes). Pick Floor (the eyedropper next to Cut Floor) lets you click a point on the model: a blue plane follows the mouse at that height, and everything below the clicked height is cut on the next Crush. The X clears it, and Cut Floor finds the floor by itself again. A ground scan (a patch of terrain) has a dense flat top of its own. That is not mistaken for a floor: only the lowest dense layer counts. Remove Spikes Two fixes in one switch: A point shot far out of the surface (farther than twice the size of its neighbour ring) is pulled back to the centre of that ring. A long stretched face, with an edge more than ten times the typical edge of the mesh, is deleted. Scanners make these where two surfaces got bridged. The small hole left behind is closed by Fill Holes. Fill Holes Small missing patches are closed. Size is the longest outline a hole may have to be filled, as a share of the model's size (default 5%). Bigger openings stay open: the bottom of a bust, the back of a relief, the edge of a ground scan. The report counts the holes filled and the openings left open. Fill Holes also handles: Cracks in scans. Scans made of many patches have thin cracks between the patches. Fill Holes zips them shut and smooths the small holes left, with no visible crack lines. A noisy rock scan comes out closed except for its outer ground edge. Only meshes that look like scans get this: hard-surface and cloth models are unchanged. It does not glue two nearby surfaces together, so you do not get edges shared by three or more faces. Flat openings of any size. Flat openings (the end of a pipe, the open side of a CAD part) are capped flat, however big. Seams are not holes. Models split along UV or material seams are not capped over the seams. Remesh uses the same crack repair on scans automatically. Order Floor, spikes and stretched faces are handled first, then small floating pieces are removed, then holes are filled, then the winding is fixed so the new faces point the right way. The crush runs on the repaired mesh. Scans keep their shading through the repair, and fine scan detail is not flattened. Scans also no longer waste triangles on the seams of their texture atlas, so more of the budget goes into the shape. Only the copy changes Clean Mesh only changes the crushed copy. Your original is never repaired or edited. When something was fixed, the report in the status bar lists it, for example how many vertices were merged and how many bad faces were removed. When to use it A crush ends far above the target and the report says the mesh may be broken: try Clean Mesh . The crushed result has holes, spikes or fragments that the original does not. The mesh comes from an AI model generator or a photogrammetry scan. If you already have Clean Mesh on and the report still says the mesh stays above the target, the mesh cannot be reduced further without breaking its shape. See Limits .

If you already have Clean Mesh on and the report still says the mesh stays above the target, the mesh cannot be reduced further without breaking its shape. See Limits .

docs.text: Hard Surface and Sharps Organic meshes (scans, sculpts) can be crushed freely. Hard-surface and CAD parts cannot. Holes must stay round, panel lines must stay straight, and material borders must stay where they are. What is kept automatically With a source of Auto , CAD or Hard Surface , these are kept in place by default, and the result still reaches the count you asked for: Edges sharper than the Hard Edge Angle (default 30°) and edges you marked Sharp. Borders between materials (not in Shape only mode, see below). Open borders (holes and cut edges). UV seams, when Textures is on. A kept edge is a cost, not a lock. The crush spends its budget everywhere else first, and when it has to touch a kept line it collapses along the crease rather than across it, so the line stays a line. Organic , Scan and Cloth sources do not keep angle-sharp edges, because on those models they are noise or folds. Edges you marked Sharp are still kept. Use Show Hard Edges (Advanced) to see the kept edges before you crush. See Show Hard Edges . Sharps Sharps is a toggle in the Keep row. It shows for Hard Surface and CAD sources, and is on by default (since 2.12.16). With Sharps on, hard edges stay in place and stay crisp after Decimate or Remesh , including corners modelled with a small bevel (a game weapon's triangle bumps, long grooves and panel lines no longer go soft). Decimate holds those edges harder while reducing, then marks the result's real creases Sharp and shades each side flat. Remesh gets one quad loop per hard edge. Small round holes come out round instead of pinched into stars, and nothing folds. Rounded parts and fillets that should look smooth are left smooth. When bevel edges cover most of a low-poly model (the game weapon), they ease off, so the result still follows the shape. It is skipped on sources over 1 million triangles (too slow there). Turn Sharps off if you want the plain method. Shape only If you switch Shading and Textures both off, you get the shape only: a closed mesh ready to 3D print. The panel says "Shape only: closed, ready to print". Clean Mesh and Fill Holes (with a big hole size) switch on by themselves, and material borders are not held. They go back as they were when you switch Shading or Textures on again. What a very low target costs Reaching the count is not free. Every kept edge is a line the crush would rather not touch, and the more of them there are, the sooner a low target forces it to. On a low-poly part with many creases, a target of a few hundred triangles means some of those lines give way: a hole loses a few sides, a chamfer flattens. The crush picks the lines that change the shape least, but check the result. If a line you care about gave way: Raise the target. Raise Hard Edge Angle , so fewer edges count as sharp. Put a Protect Area on the part that must stay. See Limits for the full list. Decimate of CAD and subdivided models CAD source: crisp corners and long thin triangles are handled, so round holes stay round and flat faces stay flat, with no streaks coming out of hole rims. Hard Surface source (a subdivided high poly): crushed with a method that keeps the rows of rounded bevels and puts big clean triangles on flat areas. A 5-million-triangle gun body takes half the time it used to. See Source Types . Flat Areas as Quads and Tidy Flat Areas (Advanced → Edges) clean up flat areas of a Decimate result. Flat Areas as Quads merges the triangles of each flat area into one face and pairs the rest into quads. Tidy Flat Areas flips long thin triangles into even ones without moving a point. They show for Auto, CAD and Hard Surface, in Decimate only.

docs.text: Import and Crush Some scans are too big to open. A 500 MB OBJ from a photogrammetry app, a PLY with ten million faces: Blender's importer takes minutes, uses many gigabytes of memory, or fails. Import and Crush skips that step. The engine reads the file itself, crushes it, and only the crushed result is built in Blender. Find it as the Import and Crush... button under Crush in the panel, or in File > Import > Polygon Crusher: Import and Crush . How to use it Click Import and Crush... and pick an .obj , .ply or .stl file. In the file browser's side panel, set the Target (Percent, Count or Triangles), Keep UVs (and textures) , Clean Mesh with its Scan Repair switches and, for OBJ files, OBJ is Y up . Click Import and Crush . The progress bar under the panel shows "Reading" while the file loads and the crush percentage after that. The result appears in the Crushed collection, named after the file, shaded smooth and selected. The report in the status bar says how many triangles the file had, how many the result has, and how long it took. A 530 MB OBJ with 8.8 million triangles reads in about a second and crushes to 100,000 triangles in about eight seconds on a desktop PC. What comes along In the file On the result OBJ vt texture coordinates, PLY per-vertex or per-face texture coordinates The UV map (with Keep UVs on) OBJ materials ( usemtl ) and the .mtl file One material per name, faces assigned as in the file map_Kd in the .mtl , or a PLY TextureFile comment The texture, connected to Base Color, when the image is next to the file and Keep UVs is on Kd colour in the .mtl The material's Base Color, when there is no texture PLY vertex colours, OBJ v x y z r g b colours A Col vertex colour layer, connected to Base Color Quads and n-gons Triangulated Normals in the file are not used: the result is shaded smooth. Faces with more than four corners are split as fans, so a concave n-gon can come out wrong. Scans do not have those. Settings that apply The file browser shows the Target , Keep UVs (and textures) , Clean Mesh with the three Scan Repair switches, and OBJ is Y up . Hard edges are used as set in the panel. Shading , Protect , Bake and LODs do not apply, because there is no original mesh in Blender to read them from. Crush the result again from the panel if you need a bake or LODs. Import and Crush always makes a triangle result (Decimate). Clean Mesh runs by itself when needed Most exported scans are split along their UV seams (every seam vertex is stored twice). Crushed as they are, they crack open along the seams. The engine checks the file and, when 2% or more of the vertices sit on another vertex, or 2% or more of the faces have no area, it runs Clean Mesh first. The report says so: "Clean Mesh ran by itself (file is split along its seams)". Textures The texture file has to be next to the model, as the .mtl or .ply names it. The add-on also looks for the file by its base name, ignoring case. When it is not found, the material is made without it and the report lists the missing names. With Keep UVs off there are no UVs to show a texture on, so the report asks you to turn it on. Tip An OBJ from most scanning apps and from Blender's own exporter is Y up. Leave OBJ is Y up on, and the model lands the way Blender's own importer would place it. For an OBJ that was written Z up, turn it off.

docs.text: LODs Tick LODs and Crush builds a full LOD chain in one click. How to use it Select the object. In Advanced → Extra Steps , tick LODs (Decimate only). Set Levels (1 to 8, default 3). Set Ratio (5% to 95%, default 50%). Click Crush LODs . The main button changes its name while LODs is on. Each level keeps Ratio of the previous level's triangles. With the default 50% ratio and three levels, the chain is: Level Triangles kept LOD0 100% (the original) LOD1 50% LOD2 25% LOD3 12.5% When an object is active, the panel lists the exact triangle count of each level under the Levels and Ratio controls. A level never has fewer than 4 triangles. What you get Objects named <name>_LOD1 , <name>_LOD2 and so on. They go in a collection named <name>_LODs , inside the Crushed collection. The original stays as LOD0 . It is not hidden and not deleted. Every level is crushed from the original , not from the level before it. This gives each level the best surface for its triangle count. What changes while LODs is on The amount (Percent, Count, Budget) is greyed out. LODs use their own Ratio. Keep Original is greyed out. LODs always keep the original. The triangle readout is hidden. Use the LOD list instead. Budget mode is not used. Each object gets its own chain. The Keep settings, Protect and Clean Mesh still apply to every level. Revert Revert works on LODs. Select an LOD object and click Revert to delete it. See Keep Original and Revert . Limits The lowest levels of a hard-surface chain are where kept edges give way and small pieces go. Check them. See Limits .

docs.text: Protect Areas Some parts of a mesh matter more than the rest: a face, hands, text on a label. Protect keeps their detail while the rest gets crushed. It is in Advanced → Extra Steps , and it only shows for Decimate . For Remesh , use Quad Density instead. How to use it In Advanced → Extra Steps , tick Protect . Then either paint it or select it. Paint it: Click Paint Protect . Blender opens Weight Paint on the protect group. Paint red where the detail must stay. Click Done Painting . Or select it: Select the object and press Tab for Edit Mode. Select the faces, edges or vertices you want to keep. Click Add . The selection goes into the protect vertex group, and the field under the buttons shows it. Remove takes selected parts back out. Add and Remove only show in Edit Mode. Then set Strength and Blur if the defaults don't suit you, turn on Show Heatmap to check the result in the viewport, and click Crush . Using your own vertex group You can also paint a vertex group yourself (Weight Paint mode, or assign weights in Edit Mode) and pick it in the field. When the active object is a mesh, the field lists its vertex groups. Higher weights keep more detail. With a group picked, Add puts the selection into that group. Strength Strength Effect 0% No protection 50% (default) Protected areas keep noticeably more detail 100% Protected areas are nearly frozen The slider is not linear. The protection grows faster as you move towards 100%. Blur Protection fades out softly from the marked area instead of stopping at a hard line. Blur sets how far, as a share of the object's size. The default is 5% . 0% makes a hard edge. Show Heatmap Colors the selected objects in the viewport by how strongly each part is protected, with the Blur fade included: blue is free to crush, red is fully protected. It updates as you add, remove or change Blur, including in Edit Mode. It is only a viewport overlay; nothing is added to your scene. Strength and Blur show once a protect group is set. Good to know The group is read after modifiers, so it matches the mesh you see in the viewport. The group name is matched on every selected object. Objects that do not have a group with that name are crushed normally. If the group exists but has no weights, the object is crushed without protection and Blender shows a warning. Protect Area works with all three target modes . Strong protection on large areas can leave the result above the target triangle count. Check the after count in the report. See Limits .

docs.text: Quad Density Quad Density lets you paint where a Remesh should use smaller or larger quads: smaller on a face, hands or a logo; larger on a flat back, the underside or parts nobody sees. It only appears while Remesh is selected. The quad count stays what you asked for. Smaller quads in the painted area mean slightly larger ones in the rest of the model, and the other way round. How to use it Under 2 Output , pick Remesh . Open Advanced → Extra Steps and tick Quad Density . Click More Detail to paint smaller quads, or Less Detail to paint larger quads. Blender opens Weight Paint on its own group ( Quad Density or Quad Density Less ). The button of the group you are painting stays pressed, and you can switch between the two. Paint red where you want the change. Soft paint gives an in-between size with a smooth change at the edge. Click Done Painting , then Crush . Strength Strength (1 to 8, default 3) says how many times smaller (More Detail) or larger (Less Detail) the quads get where you painted at full weight. 3 means up to three times. Good to know It works with a Mirror modifier (paint one half, both get it), with Symmetry , and on sewn garments and many-part models. On a scanned human with the head painted More Detail , the head came out with quads half the size (four times as many) for the same 2,000 quads overall. Painted Less Detail , the quads were almost twice as large. A part smaller than one of the big quads (fingers, a fist) loses its shape under Less Detail. Leave small parts unpainted, or lower Strength .

docs.text: Remesh (Quads) Decimate keeps the original surface and reduces its triangles. Remesh throws the old triangles away and builds the model again from clean, even quads. Use it when you want to keep editing the model, sculpt on it, subdivide it or animate it. Use Decimate when you need exact triangle counts for a game, or when the original must stay exactly as it is. Click the Remesh tab under 2 Output , set the amount, and click Crush . The main button is the same: it does the job of the tab you chose. The count you ask for is the count you get The amount works like Decimate's ( Percent , Count or Budget ) and is turned into quads: half the triangles the amount would keep. The panel shows tris → quads before you start. The quad engine on its own overshoots a target by three or four times. Polygon Crusher searches for the setting that lands on your number, and the status box under Keep tells you the real count it reached (for example "4,329 faces, 88.9% quads"). If it had to spend more quads to avoid damage, it says that too. Models made of loose parts, or parts too small for a quad, come out with a share of triangles joined into quads (often 60 to 90% quads). What is automatic Remesh has very few switches because it looks at the model and decides: CAD parts (Source: Auto, CAD or Hard Surface). If the model is made of flat faces with round holes and straight walls, it builds a clean graded grid: flat faces stay flat, every hole is a closed round loop, and the hard edges get quad loops. The quads inside flat faces are evened out. Very low counts get a coarser all-quad grid. If the model needs more quads than you asked for, the status says so (a block with many holes needs at least about 1,240). Models that are not flat faces with round holes use the general remesh. Many-part models (game weapons, kits of hundreds of parts). Each big part is remeshed on its own and checked against the original. Parts too small or thin for the quad size are simplified as triangles at their share of the budget, then paired into quads, so nothing vanishes. Sewn garments (Marvelous Designer, CLO). The panels are sewn together and remeshed in one run. Scans. Cracks between patches are closed first (the same repair as Fill Holes ), so the quads no longer show every crack. Faces pointing both ways (common in 3D-print exports). They are turned to agree first, and the shading is copied from the fixed copy, so edges do not show dark nicks. Thin walls and bars. When most walls are about as thin as a quad, the result is also built from a simplified copy and the one that fits the original better is kept. Sharp edges. Hard edges and edges you marked Sharp steer the quad loops: on a hard-surface model most of the sharp edges are followed by a loop. With Sharps on (Hard Surface and CAD sources), small round holes stay round and beveled corners stay crisp. Damage repair. If a remesh tears holes in a closed model, it tries again with more quads until the result is clean. UVs and materials. With Textures on, UVs and materials are carried to the result, and a bake is made automatically if the UV seams would leave cracks. Vertex colors are kept. A stuck engine. If the quad engine stops making progress, it is stopped and the next option is tried. The switches you have Source — pick the right one. See Source Types . Shading — the result takes the original's shading, so the surface still reads the same with far fewer faces. Textures — keep UVs and materials. With Bake to Textures on, you can also tick Bake Into Kept UVs to bake into the carried UV layout instead of a fresh unwrap. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Sharps — Hard Surface and CAD only. Symmetry — remeshes one half and mirrors it, so both sides have the same quads and the seam runs straight down the middle. It uses the axis you pick (X, Y or Z). Rebuild Surface — off by default. For hopeless input: triangle soups of loose strips, open or self-crossing models. It rebuilds a closed skin first, then remeshes it. Details finer than the skin and your Sharp marks are lost. With it off, nothing changes. Quad Density (Advanced) — paint where you want smaller or larger quads. See Quad Density . Show Hard Edges (Advanced) — see which edges the quad loops will follow. See Show Hard Edges . Keep Original works as in Decimate, with one difference: Remesh leaves the source in place, and Revert cannot go back to it when Keep Original is off (the panel shows a red warning). LODs, Clean Mesh, Protect and the flat-area options are hidden while Remesh is selected. After a Remesh the new mesh is selected and active. Best on, and not for Remesh is best on scans, sculpts, organic shapes, garments and CAD parts. On a hard-surface model with many bevels (a game weapon), Decimate with Sharps keeps the edges crisper, so use Decimate there if crisp hard edges matter more than quads. The quad engine's result differs slightly between processors (Apple Silicon and Intel, for example), because they round floating-point maths differently. On your own computer, the same model with the same settings gives the same mesh every time. Progress While it runs, the Crush button becomes Cancel with a progress bar that steps through Reading, Preparing, Remeshing, Building, Shading and Baking. The slow steps run in small pieces, so Blender keeps redrawing.

docs.text: Decimate keeps the original surface and reduces its triangles. Remesh throws the old triangles away and builds the model again from clean, even quads. Use it when you want to keep editing the model, sculpt on it, subdivide it or animate it. Use Decimate when you need exact triangle counts for a game, or when the original must stay exactly as it is. Click the Remesh tab under 2 Output , set the amount, and click Crush . The main button is the same: it does the job of the tab you chose.
docs.title: Remesh (Quads)

docs.text: The amount works like Decimate's ( Percent , Count or Budget ) and is turned into quads: half the triangles the amount would keep. The panel shows tris → quads before you start. The quad engine on its own overshoots a target by three or four times. Polygon Crusher searches for the setting that lands on your number, and the status box under Keep tells you the real count it reached (for example "4,329 faces, 88.9% quads"). If it had to spend more quads to avoid damage, it says that too. Models made of loose parts, or parts too small for a quad, come out with a share of triangles joined into quads (often 60 to 90% quads).
docs.title: The count you ask for is the count you get

docs.text: Remesh has very few switches because it looks at the model and decides: CAD parts (Source: Auto, CAD or Hard Surface). If the model is made of flat faces with round holes and straight walls, it builds a clean graded grid: flat faces stay flat, every hole is a closed round loop, and the hard edges get quad loops. The quads inside flat faces are evened out. Very low counts get a coarser all-quad grid. If the model needs more quads than you asked for, the status says so (a block with many holes needs at least about 1,240). Models that are not flat faces with round holes use the general remesh. Many-part models (game weapons, kits of hundreds of parts). Each big part is remeshed on its own and checked against the original. Parts too small or thin for the quad size are simplified as triangles at their share of the budget, then paired into quads, so nothing vanishes. Sewn garments (Marvelous Designer, CLO). The panels are sewn together and remeshed in one run. Scans. Cracks between patches are closed first (the same repair as Fill Holes ), so the quads no longer show every crack. Faces pointing both ways (common in 3D-print exports). They are turned to agree first, and the shading is copied from the fixed copy, so edges do not show dark nicks. Thin walls and bars. When most walls are about as thin as a quad, the result is also built from a simplified copy and the one that fits the original better is kept. Sharp edges. Hard edges and edges you marked Sharp steer the quad loops: on a hard-surface model most of the sharp edges are followed by a loop. With Sharps on (Hard Surface and CAD sources), small round holes stay round and beveled corners stay crisp. Damage repair. If a remesh tears holes in a closed model, it tries again with more quads until the result is clean. UVs and materials. With Textures on, UVs and materials are carried to the result, and a bake is made automatically if the UV seams would leave cracks. Vertex colors are kept. A stuck engine. If the quad engine stops making progress, it is stopped and the next option is tried.
docs.title: What is automatic

docs.text: Source — pick the right one. See Source Types . Shading — the result takes the original's shading, so the surface still reads the same with far fewer faces. Textures — keep UVs and materials. With Bake to Textures on, you can also tick Bake Into Kept UVs to bake into the carried UV layout instead of a fresh unwrap. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Sharps — Hard Surface and CAD only. Symmetry — remeshes one half and mirrors it, so both sides have the same quads and the seam runs straight down the middle. It uses the axis you pick (X, Y or Z). Rebuild Surface — off by default. For hopeless input: triangle soups of loose strips, open or self-crossing models. It rebuilds a closed skin first, then remeshes it. Details finer than the skin and your Sharp marks are lost. With it off, nothing changes. Quad Density (Advanced) — paint where you want smaller or larger quads. See Quad Density . Show Hard Edges (Advanced) — see which edges the quad loops will follow. See Show Hard Edges . Keep Original works as in Decimate, with one difference: Remesh leaves the source in place, and Revert cannot go back to it when Keep Original is off (the panel shows a red warning). LODs, Clean Mesh, Protect and the flat-area options are hidden while Remesh is selected. After a Remesh the new mesh is selected and active.
docs.title: The switches you have

docs.text: Remesh is best on scans, sculpts, organic shapes, garments and CAD parts. On a hard-surface model with many bevels (a game weapon), Decimate with Sharps keeps the edges crisper, so use Decimate there if crisp hard edges matter more than quads. The quad engine's result differs slightly between processors (Apple Silicon and Intel, for example), because they round floating-point maths differently. On your own computer, the same model with the same settings gives the same mesh every time.
